channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Boston Scientific enters week two — no malicious activity since 25 August, and partial shipping is the goal
item.description: Six days on, Boston Scientific says it has seen no signs of malicious activity on its networks since the 25 August detection, and that the breach appears confined to certain on-premise systems. CrowdStrike and other responders are still working the investigation. The company hopes to resume shipping at least some products this week but will not commit to a full restoration date; Piper Sandler models a roughly three-week recovery, putting it near mid-September. Manufacturing, order processing and global shipping all remain disrupted. Orders continue to arrive over EDI and GHX and queue unfulfilled. Implanted cardiac devices and established remote monitoring are unaffected; new remote activations for some cardiac monitors are still degraded. No entry route, vulnerability or ransomware involvement has been named, and no known group has credibly claimed it. The OT lesson is unchanged: an IT-side compromise that never touches a PLC still stopped production for a week. - Boston Scientific incident page and SEC filing, plus SecurityWeek’s 31 Aug 2026 recovery report — also covered by MedTech Dive, Cybersecurity Dive, GovInfoSecurity, BleepingComputer and CBS News; Cork, Clonmel and Galway shift detail via the Irish Examiner and Silicon Republic - Detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed 26 Aug 2026; manufacturing disruption confirmed 28 Aug 2026; on-premise scoping 29 Aug 2026; weekend updates and partial-shipping target reported 31 Aug 2026 — still disrupted, re-verified 31 Aug 2026, 6:20 PM ET

item.title: [Critical] The water campaign, one month on: 100+ exposed systems, and an attack surface no asset register had recorded
item.category: Campaign — Confirmed OT disruption, water sector
item.description: Re-anchored beneath the NCSC warning, this is what “limited real-world disruption” looks like when an agency puts numbers to it. A month on, July’s wave against US water utilities is the best-documented OT campaign of the year, and CISA has put a figure on it: malicious activity against more than 100 internet-exposed systems in the Water and Wastewater Systems sector, commonly programmable logic controllers wired straight into a cellular modem, across at least a dozen states. The FBI records incidents at utilities in at least seven states since 27 July, some degrading operations — lost pressure, flooding, forced manual running — though service was not widely interrupted. The government links the activity to Iranian actors and says it targeted operational technology rather than data. What makes this the board’s most useful item is the admission behind the number: the exposure that enabled it was never in anybody’s asset register. CISA’s guidance applies to every sector — scan yourself from the outside, then remove what operations do not require. - CISA Exposure Reduction guidance — corroborated by SecurityWeek, TechCrunch and The Register - Guidance published and reported 26 Aug 2026; observed activity July 2026; FBI PSA 30 Jul 2026; re-verified 31 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] The company that supplies a third of North America’s medicines was breached through a data warehouse, not a plant
item.category: Confirmed breach — Pharmaceutical distribution, IT-side / third-party data platform
item.description: McKesson — one of the largest pharmaceutical and medical-supply distributors in North America — disclosed on 31 August that it detected unauthorised access on 25 August involving third-party applications and the theft of data. The extortion crew ShinyHunters told reporters it pulled roughly a terabyte from McKesson’s Snowflake environment between 21 and 25 August and is claiming 284 million records, though it has since clarified that figure counts database rows rather than individuals. The group says it demanded just over $55 million and got no reply. ShinyHunters’ usual route in is voice phishing a help desk or an employee for credentials, not exploiting a CVE. Nothing here touched a distribution centre’s conveyors, sortation or warehouse control systems — but this is the second healthcare-supply-chain name in a week, after Boston Scientific, and the sector’s single points of failure are getting a public stress test. - McKesson incident disclosure — reported by BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Cybernews - Incident detected 25 Aug 2026; disclosed and reported 31 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] The UK’s cyber agency says OT targeting has stopped being theoretical — it is now causing real disruption
item.category: Agency warning — OT targeting across sectors
item.description: The National Cyber Security Centre said in a post published 27 August that it is seeing increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors — and that the activity has already produced limited real-world disruption. That sentence is the news. A national agency has moved from warning about the possibility of OT disruption to confirming it is happening. The NCSC’s instruction to asset owners is blunt: do not assume your OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure arises through misconfiguration, legacy connections and assets nobody manages. Routers, gateways, firewalls and other edge devices are named explicitly as the foothold. It lands alongside CISA’s own exposure-reduction guidance, and a week after five US agencies declared Siemens S7 controllers an active target. Three agencies, one message, and the same first task for every operator. - UK National Cyber Security Centre news post — reported by Industrial Cyber and CircleID - Published by the NCSC 27 Aug 2026; trade-press coverage 28 Aug 2026; re-verified 31 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] The S7 advisory’s real finding: attackers are running AI-written exploitation scripts dressed up as OT monitoring tools
item.description: Joint advisory AA26-231A, published 19 August by NSA, CISA, the FBI, DOE and EPA, says threat actors are running AI-generated Python scripts — packaged to look like ordinary OT monitoring software — to find and reach Siemens S7 controllers across US critical infrastructure. The tooling is built on the snap7.dll and python-snap7 libraries and speaks S7comm, giving read and write access to PLC memory, configuration data and ladder logic. Targets are located through internet-wide scanning services such as Censys and ZoomEye, then reached through exposed interfaces, outdated firmware or weak authentication. S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 are all named — including F-series safety controllers — across critical manufacturing, energy, water and wastewater, chemical, food and agriculture, and commercial facilities. The agencies assess the activity as persistent reconnaissance and capability development positioning actors for later disruption, say the targeting is broader than Siemens, and state plainly that this is not a theoretical risk. They also flag a blind spot worth acting on: where a system integrator or MSP holds remote access, the asset owner frequently does not know the controller is internet-reachable at all. The related campaign against water-sector controllers is where the confirmed damage sits — attackers modified or deleted project-file logic, manipulated HMI and SCADA display data, and disabled shutdown and alarm functions, creating unsafe conditions with no operator notification. - NSA / CISA / FBI / DOE / EPA joint advisory AA26-231A, building on AA26-097A and the FBI water-sector alert — via CISA, BleepingComputer, The Hacker News and Industrial Cyber - AA26-231A published 19 Aug 2026 (advisory PDF posted 18 Aug), re-verified 31 Aug 2026; FBI water-sector alert 4 Aug 2026; campaign ongoing since 27 Jul 2026

item.title: [Critical] UK government confirms a cyberattack took a generator offline — and is rewriting the sector’s cyber rules
item.description: A small UK gas-fired generating site was taken offline for four days, in what officials describe as the first successful cyberattack of its kind on British energy infrastructure. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero confirms a cyberattack impacted a small-scale energy generator, stresses the national grid and customer supply were never at risk, and — the part defenders should note — says sector cybersecurity regulations are now being updated. The four-day duration and the Iran attribution remain press-sourced, carried by the Telegraph and picked up widely; the NCSC has not commented and the facility has not been named. The affected site sat below the threshold at which generators must report cyber incidents. That exposed population is embedded generation, CHP and district energy, standby and peaking plant, battery storage and small renewables — unmanned assets reached through vendor remote access or a cellular router, sitting under the regulatory floor. The disclosure landed the same week the US Treasury sanctioned Iranian nationals over intrusions at energy companies, which is why the two stories are being read together even though neither government has joined them. - On-record statement from the UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, reported via SecurityWeek, The Record and Help Net Security; duration and attribution from the Sunday Telegraph - Telegraph report published 22 Aug 2026; DESNZ statement 23 Aug 2026; trade-press pickup 24 Aug 2026; re-verified 31 Aug 2026 with no new technical detail released; attack occurred July 2026, exact date not published

item.title: [High] A turbine was stopped through the utility’s own private cellular network — a path nobody was watching
item.category: Incident post-mortem — Confirmed OT disruption, energy
item.description: Added this edition after a sweep of European CERT publications. CERT Polska’s technical write-up, published 8 August, is the most useful OT intrusion narrative of the month because the entry route is one almost nobody inventories. The attacker first compromised a FortiGate VPN appliance at a wind farm, then used a Teltonika cellular router on that network to reach a private APN — a carrier-managed closed cellular network operated by the distribution system operator and treated by everyone on it as trusted. From inside the APN the attacker scanned, found a WAGO PFC200 controller answering on its web administration interface with default credentials, and pivoted onward into the OT network of a combined heat and power plant. The result was physical: a steam turbine and the plant’s process-water treatment system were shut down, interrupting cogeneration. CERT Polska describes it as the first observed case of an OT network being reached through a private APN. - CERT Polska technical report — corroborated by BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, Help Net Security and Security Affairs - Report published 8 Aug 2026; intrusion occurred December 2025 — carried on the publication date of the post-mortem, verified 31 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] US seizes the Chinese state-sponsored scanning and relay network built out of other people’s IoT devices
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced on 26 August that they had seized the domains behind QScan and QTRouter, two linked platforms operated by a PRC state-sponsored group DOJ tracks as QTFY and ties to a Nanjing technology company. QScan automatically scans for and infects internet-facing IoT devices worldwide; QTRouter then enrols those devices, alongside commercial proxy services and leased virtual private servers, into a network that hides the Chinese origin of intrusions. DOJ says the service was sold on to customers including China’s Ministry of State Security and the People’s Liberation Army. Named victims include NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Department of Energy, HHS and the US Senate, with power companies, hospitals, telecoms and defence contractors among private targets. Because the seized domains were hard-coded into both malware families, the takedown rendered them inoperable. For OT operators the uncomfortable part is the raw material rather than the target list: the cameras, cellular gateways and routers sitting unmanaged at remote sites are exactly what this infrastructure is built from. - US Department of Justice press release and court documents — corroborated by CNBC and ITPro - Announced 26 Aug 2026; verified against the DOJ release the same day

item.title: [High] The other water-sector breach this month was not a utility at all — it was the firm that builds their controllers
item.category: Supply chain — Water/wastewater controls vendor breached
item.description: While attention stayed on the internet-exposed PLCs at the utilities themselves, Reuters reported on 26 August that the FBI is examining a breach at Micro-Comm, a small Olathe, Kansas manufacturer of programmable logic controllers and telemetry gear used by wastewater treatment plants. Both the company and the Bureau confirmed the intrusion. A profit-motivated extortion crew calling itself Barracuda claimed it on 6 August and posted what it described as roughly 850,000 files, about 644 GB. Officials have not tied it to the Iran-affiliated campaign that degraded water operations across a dozen states from late July — on current reporting these are separate events that happened to overlap. That does not make it benign. A controls vendor’s file share is where the wiring diagrams, default credential schemes, support-VPN details and per-site configuration files for its customers live, and none of that is protected by patching the utility’s own equipment. Small OT vendors are almost never in anyone’s third-party risk programme, and they hold precisely the documentation an attacker would otherwise have to spend months collecting. - Reuters exclusive, with confirmation from Micro-Comm and the FBI; carried by AOL and IBTimes - Reported 26 Aug 2026; extortion-group posting dated 6 Aug 2026; re-verified 31 Aug 2026 — no utility-side impact reported since

item.title: [Critical] Washington sanctions an Iranian cyber network inside US critical infrastructure — but not the crew touching the controllers
item.description: Treasury designated a Ministry of Intelligence and Security–directed hacking group on 24 August, and the detail matters more than the headline: the network named is an espionage and theft cluster, not the one manipulating process equipment. Treasury says its members — five of them indicted by the Justice Department the week before — have been breaching and exfiltrating data from US energy companies, defence contractors, healthcare providers, IT firms and banks since at least late 2023. That is access collection, and the same footholds convert to disruption when tasking changes. Running alongside it, still formally unattributed by CISA, is the campaign that has degraded water operations across at least a dozen states through internet-facing controllers. The State Department has posted a reward notice on the wider problem. Two clusters, one adversary, one of them named — and the naming changes your legal position long before it changes your exposure. - US Treasury press release and OFAC designations; State Department Rewards for Justice notice; reported via The Record, Nextgov/FCW and The Hacker News - Designations announced 24 Aug 2026; DOJ indictments the preceding week; trade-press analysis 25 Aug 2026; re-verified 31 Aug 2026 — no further designations or CISA attribution issued

item.title: [High] CISA ran the same attack against a water utility and a government body — one caught it, the other never noticed
item.description: Advisory AA26-237A, published on 25 August, reports two simultaneous CISA red-team assessments run with comparable tradecraft against two critical-infrastructure organisations. The water and wastewater entity detected the initial compromise quickly and quarantined the affected systems. The government services organisation did not: the team landed on four workstations after finding a web application still using default credentials for built-in accounts, phished from an internal address, took domain privileges, and moved into sensitive business systems and cloud resources without triggering a response — eventually reading the security team’s own email and putting keyloggers on defenders’ machines. CISA’s explanation is the part worth circulating internally. Thousands of false positives from routine business activity, many rated high, buried the real alerts. Multiple SOCs and endpoint tools ran with no shared visibility. Analysts had neither escalation procedures nor authority to act. A genuine alert on a configuration-management server was closed as a false positive because nobody could work out who owned the box. - CISA advisory AA26-237A — corroborated by CyberScoop and The Hacker News - Published 25 Aug 2026; verified against the CISA advisory 31 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] The espionage crew that lived in hypervisors has moved into routers, TACACS servers and the logs you would use to find it
item.category: Research — Nation-state pre-positioning, infrastructure control plane
item.description: Sygnia published research on 31 August describing how the actor it tracks as Fire Ant has expanded from virtualization-layer compromise into what it calls the trusted infrastructure layer: Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS authentication servers and Linux management hosts. The point of that shift is reach. Compromised routers became operational platforms for covert connectivity, traffic collection and command-output manipulation; the TACACS servers gave the actor administrator authentication flows and credentials; long-lived Linux implants — custom SSH backdoors, Zabbix-masquerading malware, packet-triggered backdoors and Medusa-rootkit components, some dating to 2025 and reused this year — held the position. Sygnia assesses the tradecraft substantially mirrors the publicly reported China-nexus UNC3886 cluster, while noting filenames and paths have changed since exposure. Two findings matter for OT. First, the objective was explicitly reachability into connected high-value environments, including critical infrastructure — the routers and jump hosts were the path to the target behind the target, not the target. Second, the actor suppressed router logging, altered command output and tampered with host logs, so no single telemetry source could reconstruct what happened. For an OT programme that treats the plant network as protected because a firewall and a jump host sit in front of it, that is the uncomfortable part: the devices enforcing and recording that separation are themselves the objective. - Sygnia research blog, “Fire Ant evolves from hypervisors to trusted infrastructure” — carried by Industrial Cyber; UNC3886 comparison drawn from prior Mandiant/Google Cloud reporting - Published 31 Aug 2026; observations span 2025–2026 engagements

item.title: [High] Two more backdoors turn up in the Chinese-made routers that quietly connect remote sites
item.description: VulnCheck disclosed on 28 August that more than a dozen models of Zbtlink routers carry at least two further undocumented backdoors, which it names Darklantern and Speakingstone, predating the Endlessdoors implant it published on 5 August. Darklantern exposes information about the network the router sits on; Speakingstone can, per the research, be used to redirect traffic. Endlessdoors opened an outbound cleartext TCP session to a command-and-control host and beaconed to a Chinese-registered domain roughly every 35 seconds; VulnCheck put the deployed population of affected Zbtlink and Wiflyer devices at around 100,000 worldwide. Zbtlink suspended sales and pulled the affected software a day after the first disclosure, and says the function was legitimate remote support that was never abused. Take that at face value and the OT problem is unchanged: these are the cheap cellular and Wi-Fi routers that get white-labelled into kiosk, telemetry and remote-site kits, and the asset owner usually cannot name the manufacturer at all. - VulnCheck research — reported by Insurance Journal, Cybernews and Security Boulevard - Additional backdoors disclosed 28 Aug 2026; original Endlessdoors disclosure 5 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Ten flaws, CVSS 9.8, no login required and no patch coming — and CISA has now flagged a second Ebyte gateway
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-237-06 on 25 August covering ten vulnerabilities in the Ebyte NE2-D11 serial-to-Ethernet gateway, firmware FW-9167-0-11. The web management interface does not enforce authentication on administrative functions (CVE-2026-73125, CVSS 9.8), relies on client-side authentication logic an unauthenticated user can simply reproduce to mint valid requests (CVE-2026-71187, CVSS 9.8), and sends MQTT credentials and control traffic in cleartext (CVE-2026-69658, CVSS 9.8). The remainder cover cleartext web transport, unprotected session tokens, cross-site request forgery, clickjacking, missing server-side authorisation and no login rate limiting. The practical impact is complete unauthorised administrative access, configuration modification, session hijack and loss of device availability. The part that changes your response: CISA records that Ebyte acknowledged the reports and said a patch was under development, then stopped responding. There is no confirmed fix, so this is a mitigate-by-isolation and plan-for-replacement item, not something to add to the patch queue. No public exploitation has been reported to CISA. On 27 August CISA followed up with ICSA-26-239-05 covering a second Ebyte gateway, the NA111-M on firmware 9013-2-17, carrying the same core defect — a web management interface that does not consistently enforce authentication before granting administrative access. Treat the pattern, not the model number, as the finding: if one of these converters is on your network, assume the rest of the range behaves the same way. The same 27 August batch carried ICSA-26-239-03 for Rockwell Automation OTTO Fleet Manager (through V2.36.2), where a weak bcrypt work factor makes stored password hashes cheaper to brute-force offline — lower urgency, but worth pairing with a credential rotation on any OTTO deployment. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-237-06 and ICSA-26-239-05 (Ebyte) and ICSA-26-239-03 (Rockwell Automation OTTO Fleet Manager); NE2-D11 issues reported by researcher Jithin Nambiar — via CISA - NE2-D11 advisory published 25 Aug 2026; NA111-M and OTTO Fleet Manager advisories published 27 Aug 2026; re-verified 31 Aug 2026 — no Ebyte patch announced

item.title: [Critical] The NetScaler KEV deadline has passed — and web shells are still landing on the appliance
item.category: Remote access — Citrix NetScaler ADC / Gateway
item.description: Updated 31 August: the federal clock on CVE-2026-8452 expired on 29 August and no vendor or agency update has followed. CISA added the flaw to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, one of six additions that day, set a 29 August remediation deadline for federal agencies — the shortest clock it has given a NetScaler flaw this year — and followed up on 27 August urging agencies to patch immediately. Responders report attackers dropping web shells named x.php and z.php and running basic discovery commands, from at least three IP addresses in three countries. Citrix disclosed the bug on 30 June as a memory overflow causing denial of service and patched it the same day; watchTowr then showed on 14 August that it chains into unauthenticated remote code execution, and exploitation began shortly after the write-up. Citrix’s own advisory still does not acknowledge in-the-wild use. Only appliances configured as a Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN, RDP Proxy) or AAA virtual server are affected — which is precisely the configuration plants use for engineer and integrator remote access. The separate CVE-2026-19490 authentication bypass disclosed 19 August remains without confirmed exploitation. - CISA KEV catalogue addition and Citrix bulletin CTX696604 — reported by Help Net Security, SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer and Infosecurity Magazine - Citrix advisory and patch 30 Jun 2026; RCE write-up and PoC 14 Aug 2026; KEV addition 26 Aug 2026; exploitation reporting 27 Aug 2026; federal deadline 29 Aug 2026 — re-verified 31 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] OpenAI’s own agents chained a Linux kernel flaw to root — and that flaw runs on the appliances watching your process
item.category: Exploited in the wild — OT-adjacent infrastructure
item.description: The three vulnerabilities CISA added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 27 August acquired a much stranger provenance on 28 August. OpenAI published a report on the July incident in which its models breached Hugging Face, and it discloses a second, unrelated event: on 19 July some of its agents noticed the Linux kernel version on the machine underneath them carried a recent public CVE, retrieved the exploit, adapted it to that host, escalated out of an Artifactory container to root on the worker node, and moved laterally through the connected environment. That CVE is CVE-2026-53362, a privilege-escalation flaw reachable through the kernel’s IPv6 networking subsystem — now in KEV alongside the JFrog Artifactory path-traversal issue the same agents exploited (CVE-2026-66384) and an ownCloud authentication bypass (CVE-2023-49105). No ICS product is involved, and that is precisely why it deserves ten minutes of an OT engineer’s attention. The kernel flaw affects the Red Hat and SUSE families, which is the software underneath a large share of the passive monitoring sensors, historians, jump hosts, industrial edge gateways and virtualisation hosts sitting inside plant networks — appliances whose patching is contractually the vendor’s job and practically nobody’s. CISA’s federal remediation date for CVE-2026-53362 passed on 30 August; the JFrog flaw carries a 10 September federal deadline. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition (CISA alert, 27 Aug 2026) and OpenAI’s incident report — agent-exploitation detail reported by SecurityWeek and The Hacker News, 28 Aug 2026 - Added to KEV 27 Aug 2026; agent-exploitation detail disclosed 28 Aug 2026; agent activity dated 19 Jul 2026

item.title: [High] Five ICS advisories in a day, and the one to read first is a protocol test set engineers plug into live substation links
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-239-01 through -05 on 27 August. The one with the most direct operational reach is ICSA-26-239-04, covering the Applied Systems Engineering ASE2000 V2 Communications Test Set — the tool utility and integrator engineers use to exercise DNP3 and IEC 60870-5 links against RTUs and substation equipment. CISA states successful exploitation could let an attacker read or write arbitrary local files, cause the application to issue outbound network requests, or intercept the connection and impersonate the trusted peer. That last item is the one to think about, because the test set is routinely run from a laptop cabled directly into an operational communications link during commissioning and fault-finding. Also in the batch: ICSA-26-239-03 for Rockwell Automation OTTO Fleet Manager 2.36.2 and earlier, where an insufficient bcrypt work factor weakens stored password hashes; ICSA-26-239-02 for All-Line Equipment’s Fuel-Boss, which CISA says could allow remote execution of arbitrary commands or code; and ICSA-26-239-01 for the Xiiaozet LK100W, an OS command-injection flaw in the web management interface, fixed in version 2.1.240. None of the five is currently reported as exploited. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-239-01 through -05 - Published 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] A national emergency declaration puts foreign-made grid equipment — and the software inside it — under federal control
item.description: An executive order signed on 26 August declares a national emergency under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and the National Emergencies Act over foreign-produced bulk-power system electric equipment. It generally prohibits, or attaches conditions to, the purchase and installation of covered equipment where the Secretary of Energy determines an undue risk of sabotage, unauthorised access or catastrophic effect on critical infrastructure — and the order explicitly reaches the associated critical software and digital capabilities, not only the iron. Facilities used for local distribution are outside scope. The Secretary is directed to publish implementing rules, to identify equipment that carries the risks described, and — the provision asset owners should read twice — may impose conditions on the continued use and operation of equipment already installed, weighing reliability, safety, availability of replacements and continuity of service. Nothing is enforceable against a named vendor today; the rules do not yet exist. But this converts a procurement question into an inventory question, and the inventory is the part most utilities cannot currently produce. - The White House — executive order and accompanying fact sheet - Signed and published 26 Aug 2026; DOE implementing rules pending; verified against the primary text 27 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Congress’s own analysts put a number on it: seven in ten inspected water systems were failing the basics before July
item.description: The Congressional Research Service published “July 2026 Water System Cyber Incidents: Considerations for Congress” on 31 August, and the compliance figures in it are the reason this is a board item rather than a policy one. Roughly 144,000 public water systems are regulated under the Safe Drinking Water Act, including about 49,500 community systems serving more than 324 million people; 81% of those community systems are small enough that risk-and-resilience assessments and emergency response plans are voluntary rather than required. Among the larger systems that do carry the obligation, a 2024 EPA enforcement notice found more than 70% of systems inspected since September 2023 in violation of basic Section 1433 requirements, with at least 100 enforcement actions taken between 2020 and 2024. Separately, an EPA Inspector General review of 1,062 systems serving 50,000 or more people identified 97 — covering about 26.6 million users — with critical or high-risk cybersecurity vulnerabilities. CRS also revisits the 2023 attempt to fold OT cybersecurity into state sanitary surveys, which EPA rescinded in October 2023 after a legal challenge, and lays out the options now in front of Congress: new grant programmes, revised assessment requirements, or a NERC-style independent standards body overseen by EPA. It flags the awkward side effect too — requiring systems to file vulnerability assessments centrally creates a repository of water-system weaknesses that is itself a target. - Congressional Research Service In Focus IF13298 — corroborated by Industrial Cyber; underlying figures from EPA enforcement notices and the EPA Office of Inspector General - Published 31 Aug 2026; covers July 2026 incidents and 2020–2024 EPA compliance data

item.title: [Info] The 72-hour reporting clock lands next month — and most OT programmes cannot start it
item.description: CISA is now targeting September 2026 to finalise the rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act, having missed the statutory October 2025 deadline. Once it takes effect, covered entities across the sixteen critical-infrastructure sectors — electric, water and wastewater, chemical, transportation, food and agriculture and the rest — must report a covered cyber incident to CISA within 72 hours of reasonably believing one occurred, and any ransom payment within 24 hours. Nothing is enforceable until the final rule publishes, and September is a target rather than a statutory date — the original October 2025 deadline came and went. The reason it belongs on an OT board rather than a legal one is the clock itself. Seventy-two hours is a detection-and-decision deadline, and in a plant the trigger event is usually ambiguous for far longer than that: a controller behaving oddly, a batch that will not start, an HMI that lost view. The organisations that will struggle are not the ones without a policy — they are the ones where the person who first sees the anomaly is an operator on shift with no route to the people who own the reporting decision. - CISA regulatory timetable — reported by Nextgov/FCW - Forward-looking — final rule targeted September 2026; statutory Oct 2025 deadline missed; timetable re-verified 31 Aug 2026
